passages.text:
RETURNS POLICY
You can return most items within 14 days of delivery for a full refund, as long as they are unused and in their original box. Electronics must be returned within 7 days. Sale items can be exchanged but not refunded. To start a return, go to My Orders and choose 'Return item'. A driver will collect it from your address free of charge. passages.title: Groceries at the touch of a button
passages.text: More and more families in Saudi cities now buy their groceries online. Shoppers say the biggest advantage is time: instead of spending an hour in traffic and in the supermarket, they can order in ten minutes from their phone. However, not everyone is happy. Some customers complain that fruit and vegetables are not always fresh, and others miss choosing products themselves. Because of this, several apps now let customers chat with the person who is picking their order and ask for photos before the items are packed.

passages.title: The office without walls
passages.text: When Al-Dana Insurance moved its Riyadh staff into an open-plan office last year, managers expected more teamwork and faster decisions. The walls had been removed precisely so that people would talk more. What happened was almost exactly the opposite. Within months, face-to-face conversations had dropped, and the number of internal emails had nearly doubled. Employees, it seemed, put on headphones to protect themselves from the noise and then messaged the colleague two desks away rather than interrupt them. The company has not gone back to private offices, but it has added small 'quiet rooms' and asked each team to agree on hours when talking is welcome. Early results are encouraging, although the managers admit they are no longer sure what the right design is.

passages.title: Why I ignore the stars
passages.text: Online star ratings look simple enough: five stars good, one star bad. Yet anyone who has booked a hotel recently knows the system is far less helpful than it appears. Because almost every hotel now averages between 4.2 and 4.8, the difference between a good hotel and an ordinary one has all but disappeared. Many guests only leave a review when something goes badly wrong, or when the hotel offers them a discount in return. My own habit has changed as a result: I ignore the score and read the three-star reviews instead. They tend to be written by people who are neither angry nor rewarded, and they usually tell you exactly what was good and what wasn't, which is all a traveller really needs.

passages.title: The meeting nobody missed
passages.text: Few rituals of working life are as widely resented, or as stubbornly preserved, as the weekly status meeting. Ask any team and most members will tell you the hour could be replaced by a two-line email. Yet when one Jeddah logistics firm actually scrapped its Monday meeting, the results were not what its staff had predicted. Productivity barely changed; morale, on the other hand, dipped noticeably. Exit interviews later revealed that newer employees in particular had relied on the meeting not for information, which they could indeed have read elsewhere, but for a sense of who was who and whose opinion carried weight. The firm has since reinstated a shorter version, though it now calls it a 'team check-in' – a change of name that, one manager admits, has fooled nobody. The lesson, perhaps, is not that meetings are better than we think, but that we tend to misjudge what they are for.

passages.title: Too old to learn?
passages.text: It has become something of a commonplace that adults are poor language learners, and that anyone who did not start as a child should resign themselves to a lifetime of embarrassing mistakes. The research, however, paints a rather more complicated picture. Children do enjoy a clear advantage in one area: accent. Given enough exposure, they come to sound like native speakers in a way few adults ever will. In almost every other respect – vocabulary, grammar, reading, even listening – adults who study seriously tend to progress faster, at least in the early years, precisely because they can draw on what they already know. What adults lack is rarely ability; it is time, and the willingness to sound foolish in public. The first can be scheduled. The second, unfortunately, cannot, and it is this, far more than age, that seems to separate those who succeed from those who quietly give up.
